newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Luxembourg gears up to take EU presidency baton.
newsitem.headline: Luxembourg gears up to take EU presidency baton.

text.p: As the Dutch European Union presidency pulls out all the stops to secure a new EU treaty, Luxembourg is gearing up for its six months in the hot seat when preparations for eastward expansion will move to centre stage.

The new presidency will also have to work on the detailed phrasing and formulation of the latest treaty which is due to be agreed at the EU's summit in Amsterdam on Monday and Tuesday, as well as ensuring Europe's move towards a single currency remains firmly on track.

"Much of the Luxembourg agenda will be written at the Amsterdam summit," a Luxembourg government source told Reuters. The union's smallest member, with a population of just 413,000, takes up the six-month presidency on July 1.

Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Slovakia, Slovenia, Estonia, Lithuania, Latvia, Bulgaria and Romania have all been offered eventual membership of the wealthy 15-nation EU bloc, and on July 16 the European Commission is due to publish its recommendations on their readiness to join.
"Luxembourg will have to prepare the strategy for the enlargement negotiations as well as their content. This is going to be the major topic (of the presidency)," the government source said.

"It has to be decided if negotiations will start with some countries, or with all the countries and if there would then be a differentiation afterwards, so these are highly political questions as well," he added.

Membership talks with some of the 10 central and eastern European candidates are scheduled to begin six months after the Amsterdam treaty is signed, and it is expected the Luxembourg summit in December will decide which ones these will be.

The draft treaty set to be agreed at Amsterdam, the result of 15-months of inter-governmental conference (IGC) negotiations, aims to modernise the internal workings of the union in preparation for its ambitious expansion plan.
It proposes streamlining the EU decision-making process and allowing for some countries to move more easily towards closer integration if they wish without being held back by others.
It also promises EU citizens a broad range of freedoms in a more secure Europe, with protection against discrimination and job creation a formal goal.

With a decision due in April or May next year on which countries will initially take part in the single European currency set to be introduced on January 1, 1999, monetary union will obviously remain a top concern for the presidency.
"Economic and monetary union (EMU) is the last big ambition of Europe in this century and obviously there's a lot of nervousness about," the government source said.
"The Dutch presidency has had to deal with it although it was not on the agenda at all -- so EMU is always a topic that could come up with force at any time."

For Luxembourg Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker, who also acts as labour and finance minister in the country's left- leaning coalition government, addressing European social issues will be a personal priority during the presidency.

"He will table some proposals going a little further in the social dimension of Europe by introducing social minimum standards as far as labour laws are concerned. Also the social dimension is going to be important in the framework of enlargement as well," the source said.
Another potentially sensitive area for Luxembourg, a banking centre and renowned tax haven, would be further discussion of common tax possibilities in Europe.
Luxembourg, one of the founding EU members, last held the presidency in 1991, when the bulk of discussions on the Maastricht treaty on economic and monetary union took place.
